Going claim by claim.

## Claim 1 — Webinars cause 31% higher retention → make them mandatory

**Defect A: Survivorship bias in the sample definition.**
The population is "412 customers who are still active on the Pro plan today" — i.e., everyone who already churned has been excluded *before* the comparison is made. Restricting to survivors and then comparing a retention-related outcome within that survivor-only group is close to conditioning on the outcome itself. It tells you nothing reliable about whether webinar attendance predicts staying vs. churning across the full customer base, because anyone who churned (webinar attendee or not) was dropped from the analysis entirely. This would cause the reported 31% figure to be biased in an unknown direction/magnitude, so acting on it could target the wrong lever.

**Defect B: Correlation treated as causation, with an obvious confound.**
Webinar attendance is opt-in, not randomly assigned. Customers who are already more engaged, better resourced, or more committed to succeeding with the product are simultaneously more likely to (a) sign up for a webinar and (b) stick around — regardless of what the webinar itself contains. Nothing in the memo rules out this common-cause explanation (or reverse causation: customers already planning to invest in the product attend webinars). The leap from "attendees retain better" to "webinars cause retention" is unsupported. This would cause the company to spend money mandating webinars for a benefit that may not exist — and mandatory attendance changes the population (it now includes unmotivated customers who wouldn't have opted in), so even if the original correlation were real, there's no guarantee it survives once attendance is compulsory.

## Claim 2 — Central region churns less (p=0.04) → concentrate spend there

**Defect: Multiple-comparisons / data-dredging problem, uncorrected.**
Eighteen attributes were tested against churn, and the one that happened to cross the conventional p<0.05 threshold is being reported as a real finding. With 18 independent tests at α=0.05, the probability of getting at least one "significant" result purely by chance is roughly 1−0.95¹⁸ ≈ 60%, even if none of the 18 attributes actually matter. No correction (Bonferroni, FDR, etc.) is mentioned, and no effect size or confidence interval is given — only a bare p-value close to the cutoff. This is close to textbook p-hacking: run many tests, report the one that "worked." This would cause the company to reallocate real budget toward chasing statistical noise, with a good chance the "Central region effect" fails to replicate next quarter.

(A secondary, related point: even if the effect is real, region could simply be a proxy for something else — e.g., industry mix, company size, or customer tenure concentrated in that region — so "concentrate spend on Central region" may not address whatever the actual driver is. I'd fold this into the same finding rather than treat it as independent.)

## Claim 3 — Satisfaction 62%→66% shows the new support model is working

**Defect: Uncontrolled before/after comparison presented as causal proof.**
This is a single pre/post measurement with no control group, no counterfactual, and — unlike the churn claim — not even a significance test, sample size, or confidence interval attached to the 4-point change. Nothing rules out seasonality, other concurrent initiatives, measurement/survey changes, or ordinary quarter-to-quarter noise as the real explanation. A before/after delta alone cannot establish that the support model specifically caused the change. This would cause the company to credit (and keep funding) an intervention that may have had little or nothing to do with the observed improvement, while the actual cause goes unidentified.

*(Minor, secondary note: "4% improvement" is ambiguous — 62%→66% is a 4 percentage-point rise but a ~6.5% relative increase. Not a major defect on its own, but worth tightening since it's easy to misquote the magnitude later.)*

## Summary
Every one of the three conclusions outruns its evidence in a different way: Claim 1 combines survivorship bias with an unaddressed confound; Claim 2 is an uncorrected multiple-comparisons result; Claim 3 is a causal claim resting on a single uncontrolled before/after delta. None of the underlying numbers are disputed — the defects are all in the inferential leap from data to recommendation.
